article.title: Where Did Black Los Angeles Go? The Disappearance of a Community That Built the City
article.author: Sharon Kyle
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Part Two of Who Gets to Lead Los Angeles? Los Angeles celebrates its diversity. Its leaders routinely invoke the contributions of the many communities that have shaped the city. But something extraordinary has happened to one of those communities. Black Los Angeles has been disappearing. In 1980, approximately 496,000 Black people lived in Los Angeles, representing nearly 17 percent of its population. By 2020, that number had fallen to approximately 367,000, or about 9 percent. The city lost more than one-quarter of its Black population even as its overall population grew. Those numbers represent families leaving neighborhoods, businesses losing customers, churches losing congregants, and communities losing political influence. But the disappearance of Black Los Angeles is more than a demographic story. I believe it was an early warning of the economic insecurity now threatening millions of Americans. And the warning concerns not only what happened to Black Angelenos, but also what their experience reveals about how power and wealth accumulate. A Community That Helped Build Los Angeles People of African ancestry were among the city's original settlers in 1781. Of the 44 settlers who established the Spanish pueblo on Indigenous land, 26 had some African ancestry. Generations later, Black migrants from the South helped transform Los Angeles into an industrial powerhouse. They worked in aircraft manufacturing, defense production, transportation, and other industries while confronting discrimination in employment and housing. Black entrepreneurs established businesses, newspapers, churches, and cultural institutions. Central Avenue became a nationally significant center of Black music and commerce. South Los Angeles and Crenshaw became centers of political organizing and community life. Black leaders, including Mayor Tom Bradley, helped reshape city government. Black Angelenos were among the people who built modern Los Angeles. So why did so many leave? When Economic Security Disappeared For much of the twentieth century, industrial employment offered working-class families a path toward stability. Many jobs provided wages and benefits that made homeownership and a measure of financial security possible. Union contracts established wage scales, seniority protections, grievance procedures, and rules governing promotions and dismissal. Unions were not free of racial discrimination. But where Black workers gained meaningful representation, collective bargaining helped limit employers' ability to make arbitrary decisions. As manufacturing jobs disappeared, that economic foundation weakened. Factories closed, production moved elsewhere, and technological changes reduced demand for labor. Employers and policymakers also embraced arrangements that diminished workers' bargaining power. Black workers, already disadvantaged by discriminatory employment practices and unequal access to accumulated wealth, were especially vulnerable. For families with limited savings, losing a stable job could mean losing the ability to remain in Los Angeles. Meanwhile, housing costs continued rising. Many Black families moved to the Antelope Valley, the Inland Empire, and other communities where homes were more affordable. Some left voluntarily in pursuit of new opportunities. Others faced economic pressures that made remaining increasingly difficult. The distinction matters. But so does the larger pattern: a community that helped build Los Angeles was finding it harder to afford living here. Housing Discrimination Did Not End When It Became Illegal Housing discrimination compounded these pressures. For decades, racially restrictive covenants, discriminatory lending, and exclusionary real estate practices prevented Black families from accessing neighborhoods and building housing wealth available to white families. But it would be misleading to suggest that discrimination ended when fair-housing laws were enacted and only its economic consequences remained. The discrimination itself continued. I know this firsthand. In 1973, when I was 16, I participated in a high school experiment in Lakewood, California, designed to test racial discrimination in apartment rentals. A white female classmate and I posed as recent college graduates seeking apartments. We visited the same four apartment complexes separately, with me going first. At every location, I was told the apartment had already been rented. When my white classmate visited those same properties, all four accepted her application. At one complex, the manager who had told me the apartment was unavailable invited her inside to see the vacant unit. This happened five years after Congress passed the Fair Housing Act. The managers had been polite to me. Their discrimination was concealed beneath ordinary courtesy. My classmates were excited that our experiment had produced compelling evidence. But I was beginning to understand something far more personal. We had documented obstacles I could expect to encounter throughout my life. My white classmate received opportunities denied to me, although our supposed qualifications were identical. She had done nothing to earn that advantage. I had done nothing to deserve the disadvantage. The experience taught me that making discrimination illegal does not eliminate the willingness to discriminate. And when discriminatory conduct goes unchallenged, those responsible can continue benefiting from it. Black Los Angeles Was the Miner's Canary In the book, The Miner's Canary , Lani Guinier and Gerald Torres used the canary once carried into coal mines as a metaphor for racial inequality. When the canary showed signs of distress, miners knew the air was becoming dangerous. The problem was not confined to the bird. It was a warning to everyone in the mine. I believe Black Los Angeles served a similar function. For decades, Black families experienced disappearing industrial jobs, weakening labor protections, persistent housing discrimination, and rising living costs. Many eventually left the city. Today, in 2026, Americans across racial lines are confronting versions of that same insecurity. Stable employment no longer guarantees financial stability. Homeownership is increasingly difficult for younger generations. Housing costs consume household incomes while workers struggle to keep wages aligned with living expenses. The experiences are not identical. Black Angelenos faced particular forms of racial exclusion that cannot be erased by comparisons with broader economic hardship. But the underlying vulnerabilities should look familiar. The warning signs were visible long before economic insecurity became so widespread. Why didn't more Americans recognize them? The Foothold: How Power Gains More Power Martin Luther King Jr. wrote in his Letter from Birmingham Jail that “injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.” For much of my life, I understood those words primarily as a moral appeal: we should care about injustice even when it happens to someone else. I have come to understand King's warning in a more expanded way. It is also a warning about the nature of those who perpetrate injustice. People willing to exploit others, who demonstrate little regard for the suffering they cause, do not necessarily possess an internal boundary preventing them from extending that exploitation to others. Why should we assume they will stop? That question sits at the forefront of my mind when I think about Donald Trump. In 1973, the same year I discovered racial discrimination in apartment rentals through my high school experiment in California, the U.S. Department of Justice sued Donald Trump, his father Fred Trump, and their real estate company for allegedly discriminating against Black apartment seekers in New York. Federal investigators documented Black applicants being told that apartments were unavailable while white applicants were offered vacancies. The case ended in a 1975 consent decree requiring changes to the company's rental practices, although the Trumps denied wrongdoing and admitted no liability. I find the historical parallel difficult to ignore. More than fifty years later, Donald Trump occupies the most powerful political office in the country. I cannot claim that the housing discrimination allegations of 1973 shed light on every decision he has made since. But I can ask why Americans should disregard that history when evaluating how he exercises power today. For me, this is not simply a question about whether someone harbors racial animus. It is a question about what we should learn when a person or institution is credibly accused of exploiting people with limited power—and what happens when that person subsequently acquires vastly greater power. The people who are easiest to exploit today are not necessarily the only people who will be vulnerable tomorrow. That is precisely why I believe Martin Luther King Jr.'s warning deserves to be understood not only as a moral principle, but as a warning about power itself. That question is at the heart of what I call my Foothold Theory . Related: Foothold Theory: How Authoritarian Power Erodes Rights by Targeting the Least Protected First Those seeking to accumulate power and wealth often find their easiest opportunities among people with the least ability to resist. These populations are the low-hanging fruit. They may be politically marginalized, economically vulnerable, or already regarded with suspicion or contempt. Existing prejudice makes their mistreatment easier to justify. The public may be persuaded that the victims deserve their circumstances, exaggerate their suffering, or pose a threat requiring extraordinary measures. Once those justifications succeed, the exploiters gain a foothold. They establish that protections can be weakened, rights disregarded, and certain people made to bear burdens others would never accept. They also discover what the public will tolerate. The immediate victims suffer, but those responsible may gain something more enduring: wealth, political influence, institutional power, or precedents that enable further exploitation. And there is no reason to assume their ambitions will remain confined to their original targets. Those people were simply the easiest place to begin. This does not mean every injustice is part of a coordinated conspiracy or that every economic decision causing harm reflects malicious intent. But we should judge powerful people and institutions by their conduct, what they gain, and whether they seek to weaken safeguards protecting others. When those entrusted with power demonstrate a willingness to exploit people who cannot effectively resist, we should not mistake the vulnerability of their first victims for a limit on their ambitions. The Danger Does Not Stay Contained Consider housing. For generations, racial exclusion enabled some Americans to accumulate property wealth while denying others similar opportunities. Today's housing affordability crisis has additional causes, including insufficient construction, restrictive land-use policies, and the growing importance of inherited wealth. But the history reveals what happens when powerful interests protect economic advantages while others are denied a basic necessity. Labor offers another example. When workers lose collective bargaining power, employers gain greater discretion over wages, benefits, and working conditions. Black workers were especially vulnerable to discrimination and industrial displacement. But weakened labor protections do not threaten only Black workers. They affect employees across racial lines. The 2007–2008 foreclosure crisis offers an especially stark illustration. Black and Latino borrowers were disproportionately exposed to predatory and high-cost mortgage lending. When the housing market collapsed, those communities suffered devastating losses. But the consequences spread throughout the national economy. The crisis had multiple causes. Nevertheless, the treatment of vulnerable borrowers revealed dangers within a financial system willing to profit from risks others would ultimately bear. The warning was there. Too many people treated it as someone else's problem. Why This Matters to Political Leadership This article is part of a larger examination of political leadership, historical knowledge, and responsibility in Los Angeles. In Part 1, I questioned what it means when someone seeking to become mayor demonstrates an inadequate appreciation of the history of Black Angelenos and their relationship with the LAPD. The issue was never simply remembering names or dates. It was understanding how institutions acquire power, how that power has been exercised, and who suffers the consequences. The disappearance of Black Los Angeles raises the same question in the economic sphere. A mayor cannot single-handedly reverse decades of racial discrimination, restore manufacturing jobs, or eliminate economic inequality. But the mayor of Los Angeles is not powerless. The mayor helps determine the city's budget priorities, appoints department leaders and commissioners, influences housing and development policies, and oversees agencies responsible for enforcing important local protections. Those responsibilities have real consequences. A mayor who understands the history of housing discrimination can strengthen the city's response to discriminatory practices and support policies that expand access to affordable housing. A mayor who appreciates the importance of labor protections can prioritize enforcement of wage laws, protect workers from retaliation, and support stronger standards for employers doing business with the city. And a mayor who recognizes how powerful interests exploit vulnerable populations can scrutinize development decisions, public contracts, and policies that transfer economic benefits to the powerful while imposing costs on those least able to bear them. None of these powers is unlimited. The City Council, state and federal governments, courts, and private economic forces all shape what a mayor can accomplish. But those limitations make sound judgment more important, not less. Historical knowledge is not an ornament of political leadership. It is a tool for recognizing danger. Without it, leaders may mistake exploitation for ordinary economic activity, discrimination for individual misfortune, and the concentration of wealth and power for inevitable progress. The question is not whether a mayor can solve every problem. It is whether the person entrusted with the city's executive authority understands these problems well enough to recognize when government is helping perpetuate them—and has the judgment and determination to use the powers of the office to challenge them. The Warning We Failed to Hear The disappearance of Black Los Angeles is not simply a story about a community losing its foothold in a city it helped build. It is a warning about what happens when economic security erodes, discrimination persists, and those benefiting from unequal arrangements accumulate still more wealth and power. What if we had recognized the struggles of Black communities as warnings about the direction of the entire society? What if we had paid attention not only to those suffering, but also to those benefiting from their vulnerability? The Miner's Canary tells us to pay attention when vulnerable populations begin to suffer. My Foothold Theory tells us to pay attention to those willing to cause or tolerate that suffering—and to the power they gain when society allows them to proceed. One identifies the warning. The other helps explain how the danger expands. Ignorance of how power gains more power, and how wealth concentrates in the hands of those willing to exploit others, endangers us all. The question is no longer simply where Black Los Angeles went. It is whether America will recognize what its disappearance was telling us before still more communities experience the same loss of economic security. And whether the people we entrust with political power understand enough about that history to prevent the pattern from continuing.
